label: realQuadodd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{realQuadodd} Let $F$ be a real quadratic field. The class number of $F$ is odd   if and only if it takes one of the following forms:
		\begin{enumerate}[$    1)$]
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p})$ where $p$  is a   prime number congruent to $1\pmod 4$. 
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2})$  where  $q$, $q_1$, $q_2$ are prime  numbers congruent to $3\pmod 4$.
		\end{enumerate}

label: realQuadeven1New
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{realQuadeven1New}
		Let $F$ be a real quadratic field $F$. Then $h_2(F)=2$ if and only if $F$ takes one of the following forms:
		\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pq})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2pq})$  with  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p\equiv5\pmod8$.
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1q_2})$ with $q_1\equiv3\pmod8$ or $q_2\equiv3\pmod8.$
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pq_1q_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1.$
			
			
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2p})$ with $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4]$.	
			
			
			\item $F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4]$.
			
			
			
		\end{enumerate}
		Here $p\equiv 1 \pmod4$ and $q\equiv q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers.

label: realBiquad
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{realBiquad} Let $K$ be a real biquadratic number field. The class number of $K$ is odd if and only if   it takes one of the following forms:
			\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
				\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q})$,   $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{q_2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1},\sqrt{2q_2})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2},\sqrt{q_2q_3}),$
				
				\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q},\sqrt{p})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q},\sqrt{p})$ with $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p\equiv5 \pmod 8$,
				\item	$K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q_1q_2})$ with   $q_1\equiv3 \pmod 8$ or $q_2\equiv3 \pmod 8$, 
				\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{q_1q_2})$  with $\left(\frac{q_1}{p}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{q_2}{p}\right)=-1$,
				
				\item  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p})$ with $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4]$.
				
				\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4]$.
			\end{enumerate}
			Here, $p$, $p_1$, $p_2$  denote  primes numbers congruent to $1\pmod 4$ and $q$, $q_1$, $q_2$ denote  primes numbers congruent to $3\pmod 4$.

title: \bf Definition
body_md: A number field $k$  is said QO-field if it is a quadratic extension of certain number field $k'$ whose class number is odd. We shall call $k'$ a base field of the QO-field $k$ and that $k/k'$ is a QO-extension. An extension of  QO-fields is an extension of number fields $L/M$ such that $L$ and $M$ are QO-fields.

body_md: \label{squarenot}We say that $\sqrt{\varepsilon_d }$, the square-root of the fundamental unit of  a real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ equals $[\sqrt{m_1},\sqrt{m_2}]$, where $m_1$ and $m_2$ are two positive integers (i.e,  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_d }=[\sqrt{m_1},\sqrt{m_2}]$), if $\sqrt{\varepsilon_d }=n_1\sqrt{m_1}+n_2\sqrt{m_2}$ for some     integers or semi-integers  $n_1$ and $n_2$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{classqrs}
	Let $q\equiv3\pmod{4}$   be a prime number    and $d$ a positive square-free integer co-prime with $q$. Put 
	$K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q},\sqrt{d})$.
	Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $d$ is in one of the following forms:
	\begin{enumerate}[$A)$]
		\item $d=r$, where  $r\equiv1\pmod 8$ is a prime number such that     $\left(\frac{r}{q}\right)=1$ and  
		$h_2(qr)=4$.  
		\item  $d=rs$, where $r$ and $s$ are prime numbers such that,
		after a suitable permutation of $r$  and $s$, we have one of the following conditions:
		\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
			\item $r\equiv5\pmod{8}$, $ s \equiv3\pmod{4}$, and
			\[
			\left(\left(\frac{q}{r}\right),\left(\frac{q}{s}\right),
			\left(\frac{r}{s}\right)\right)
			\in\{(i,j,k):i,j,k=\pm1\}
			\setminus\{(1,1,1),(1,-1,1)\},
			\]
			                         
			
			\item    $r\equiv1\pmod{8}$, $ s \equiv3\pmod{4}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,
			                         
			\item $r\equiv q \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $s\equiv3\pmod4$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
			                         
			\item  $r\equiv s \equiv 3\pmod{8}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
			
			                         
			
			\item  $s\equiv7\pmod8, q \equiv 3\pmod{8}$, $r\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,
			
			                         
			
			\item $s\equiv3\pmod8, q \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $r\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,
			
			                         
			
			
			\item $r\equiv1\pmod8, s \equiv 5\pmod{8}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,
			
			
			                         
			\item $r\equiv s\equiv5\pmod8$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
			                         
			\item $r\equiv1\pmod8, s\equiv5\pmod8,q\equiv3\pmod8$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$.
			
			
			
			
		\end{enumerate}	
		\item $d=2p$, where $p\equiv 5\pmod8$  is a prime number.
		\item $d=2q'$, where $q'\equiv 3\pmod4$ is a prime number   such that $q$ or $q'$ is congruent to $3\pmod8.$
		
	\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
$\bullet$ Let us firstly note that if $h_2(K)=2$ and $d$ is odd, then the rank of the $2$-class group of $K$ equals  $1$; and so,
	according to \cite[Lemma 3.1]{ChemseddinGreenbergConjectureI},   $d$ is in one of the following forms:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $d=r$ is a prime number such that $r\equiv1\pmod 8$ and  $\left(\frac{r}{q}\right)=1$,
		\item  $d=rs$ where $r$ and $s$ are two distinct prime numbers.
	\end{enumerate}
	Assume that $d$ takes the first form (i.e. as in $a)$). So the extension $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qr})$ is an unramified quadratic extension. Since the $2$-class group of 
	$	\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qr})$ is cyclic (cf. \cite[Corollary 18.6]{conner88}), it follows that
	$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if 
	$h_2(qr)=4$ (this justifies the form $A)$). 
	
	
	Now assume that $d$ takes the second form (i.e. as in $b)$). Let us characterize  the integers $d$ such that $h(K)=2$. Put $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qrs})$. We distinguish the following two cases: 
	
	\noindent\ding{229}	 	Assume that $K/k$ is  {ramified}, i.e., $rs\equiv 3\pmod4$. So $h_2(k)$ divides $h_2(K)$, and thus   $h_2(k)=1$ or $2$.  The case $h_2(k)=1$ is rejected as  $h_2(k)$ is divisible by $2$   (cf. \cite[Corollary 18.6]{conner88}). Therefore, $h_2(k)=2$;
	                                       
		           
		                
	and so, by Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}, we have	$q\equiv s \equiv3 \pmod4$ and $r\equiv1\pmod4$ with $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=-1$.  We distinguish two sub-cases:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $r\equiv5\pmod 8$. 
		Using Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8}, and Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo}),   we check that $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_q,\varepsilon_{rs},\eta(r,s,q)\rangle}$, where $\eta(r,s,q)$ is as in Table \ref{formofeta}:
		\begin{table}[H]  
			\centering
			\scriptsize                                                                                       
			\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}                                                                         
			\renewcommand{1.3}{1.3}                                                          
			\begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c|c}
				\toprule
				$\left(\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right),\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right),\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)\right)$ & $\eta(5,7,3)$ & $\eta(5,3,3)$ & $\eta(5,3,7)$& $\eta(5,7,7)$\\
				\midrule
				$(1,1,-1)$	&  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ &  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$&$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$\\
				\hline
				$(-1,-1,1)$  &  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$& $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$\\
				\hline
				$(-1,-1,-1)$  & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$& $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ &$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ \\
				\hline
				$(-1,1,1)$ &  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ &  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$&$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$\\
				\hline
				$(-1,1,-1)$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs} \varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$&$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$\\
				\hline
				$(1,-1,-1)$   & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ &  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$& $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{rs}\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ &$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ \\
				\bottomrule
			\end{tabular}
			\caption{The form of $\eta(r,s,q)$}
			\label{formofeta}
		\end{table}
		
		
		Thus,	 $q(K)=2$.
		Since $h_2(rs)=h_2(qrs)=2$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}), it follows  by Kuroda's class number formula that we have $h_2(K)=2$ (this justifies the form $B)$-$1)$).	
		\item Now let $r\equiv1\pmod 8$. According to Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}, $[h_2(qrs)=2$ and $h_2(rs)=2]$  if and only if  $\left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=-1$. Furthermore, from
		Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8},  we deduce that $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_q,\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{rs}},\eta\rangle}$ where $\eta=\varepsilon_{qrs}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{qrs}}$ according to whether $\left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=-1$ or not.  Therefore, 
		$q(K)=2$ exactly when $\left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-1$.
		It follows, by  Kuroda's class number formula  (cf. \eqref{equa1}), that    $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)= \left(\dfrac{s}{r}\right)=-1$ (this justifies the form $B)$-$2)$).
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\noindent\ding{229} 	Now assume that  $K/k$ is unramified, i.e., $rs\equiv1\pmod 4$. We distinguish two sub-cases: 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Let $r\equiv s\equiv 3\pmod4$, then   \cite[Theorem 1]{BS95} implies that $k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}$. Therefore, 
		                           
		$	h_2(K)=\frac{h_2(k)}{2}; $
		                
	and thus $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $h_2(k)=4$. Under the  conditions of this sub-case, the   quadratic fields $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qrs})$ such that $h_2(k)=4$ can be deduced from \cite[Form $d_i$, for $i\in \{1,...,8\}$, page 11]{BS25I}. In fact, we have $h_2(k)=4$ if and only if,    after a suitable permutation of the prime numbers  $q,r$ and $s$, we have $\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{s}{q}\right)=1$ and one of the    conditions in Table \ref{refddd} :
	
	
	\begin{center}
		\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
		\begin{table}[H]
			\begin{tabular}{c|ccc|c}
				
				\toprule
				Cas
				& $r \pmod{8}$
				& $s \pmod{8}$
				& $q \pmod{8}$  &  $\left(\dfrac{r}{q}\right)$ \\
				\midrule
				$d_{1}$ & $7$ & $7$ & $7$ &  $-1$ \\
				$d_{2}$ & $7$ & $3$ & $7$ & $-1$  \\
				$d_{3}$ & $3$ & $3$ & $7$ & $-1$  \\
				$d_{4}$ & $3$ & $3$ & $3$ & $-1$ \\
				$d_{5}$ & $7$ & $3$ & $7$ & $1$\\
				$d_{6}$ & $7$ & $7$ & $3$ & $1$ \\
				$d_{7}$ & $3$ & $7$ & $3$ & $1$  \\
				$d_{8}$ & $3$ & $3$ & $7$ & $1$  \\
				\bottomrule
				
			\end{tabular}
			\caption{Conditions on $r$, $s$ and $q$ ensuring $h_2(qrs)=4$ in case $r\equiv s\equiv3\pmod4$.}
			\label{refddd}
		\end{table}
	\end{center}
	This justifies the   forms listed from $B)$-$3)$ to $B)$-$6)$.
	
	
	\item Let $r\equiv s \equiv 1\pmod4$. Notice that  if  $h_2(K)=2$, then the class field tower of $k$ is abelian, i.e., $k^{(1)}= k^{(2)}$. Thus,  using the classification in \cite[Form $c_i$, for $i\in \{15,...,20\}$, page 177-178]{BS95}, by interpreting the graphs corresponding to the abelian case to those of type 7  (for a definition of these graphs reader can see page 168 in the same reference), we deduce that $r$, $s$ and $q$ satisfy one of the conditions in Table \ref{qrsabelien}:
\end{enumerate}

\begin{center}
	\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
	\begin{table}[H]
		\begin{tabular}{c|ccc|ccc}
			\toprule
			Cas
			& $r \pmod{8}$
			& $s \pmod{8}$
			& $q \pmod{8}$ & $\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)$
			& $\left(\dfrac{r}{q}\right)$ &  $\left(\dfrac{s}{q}\right)$ \\
			\midrule
			$c_{15}$ & $1$ & $5$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $-1$ & $1$ \\
			$c_{16}$ & $1$ & $5$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $-1$&$1$  \\
			$c_{17}$ & $5$ & $5$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $-1$ &$-1$ \\
			$c_{18}$ & $1$ & $5$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $-1$  &$-1$\\
			$c_{19}$ & $5$ & $5$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $1$  &$-1$\\
			$c_{20}$ & $5$ & $5$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $1$  &$-1$ \\
			\bottomrule
		\end{tabular}
		
		\caption{Conditions on $r$, $s$ and $q$ ensuring $h_2(qrs)=4$ in abelian $2$-tower case and $r\equiv s\equiv1\pmod4$} \label{qrsabelien}
	\end{table}
\end{center}

So let us assume that $q$, $r$ and $s$ satisfy one of the conditions presented in Table  \ref{qrsabelien}.
Notice that $h_2(qrs)=4$ and  since in all  cases we have $\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,  it follows that $h_2(rs)=2$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}). Thus, by Kuroda's class number formula,  $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $q(K)=1$.


On the other hand, using  Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8}, we check that  $E_K=\langle-1, \varepsilon,\varepsilon,\varepsilon\text{ or } \sqrt{\varepsilon}  \rangle$ according to whether $[r\equiv s\equiv5\pmod8, q\equiv7\pmod8   \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{s}{q}\right)=-1]$ or not. Hence, $h_2(K)=4$ or $2$, more precisely,
\begin{equation*}
	h_2(K)=4 \text{ if and only if } r\equiv s\equiv5\pmod8, q\equiv7\pmod8   \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{s}{q}\right)=-1.
\end{equation*}
Which 		  justifies the   forms listed from $B)$-$7)$ to $B)$-$9)$.




\indent$\bullet$	Finally let $d$ be an even positive square-free integer co-prime with $q$, i.e.,   $d=2d'$, where $d'$ is an odd positive square-free integer (co-prime with $q$). Notice that if $h_2(K)=2$, then the fact that the extension $K/\mathbb{Q}(2qd')$ is ramified, implies that  $h_2(2qd')\in\{1,2\}$. It follows, by Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}, that the integer $d'$ is in one of the following sub-cases:   $[d'=1]$, $[d'=p  \text{ is a prime number with }  p\equiv5\pmod8   \text{ or }  \left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)=-1]$ or $[d'=q' \;\text{ is a prime numer with }   q'\equiv3\pmod8]$. 


We note that the sub-case $d'=1$  is eliminated, as it implies, by  Lemma \ref{realBiquad},  that $h_2(K)=1$.
So let us assume that $d'=p$ is a prime number with  $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or  $\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)=-1$. If $p\equiv5\pmod8$, then $h_2(2p)=h_2(2pq)=2$ (cf. Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}); and on the other hand, we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_q,\varepsilon_{2p}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{2pq}}\rangle}$ (cf. Table \ref{tab7}), i.e.,  $q(K)=2$.
Thus, by Kuroda's class number formula, we have $h_2(K)=2$.  This justifies the form $C)$.

Now  let  $p\equiv1\pmod8$ and $\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)=-1$. So we have $q(K)\geq 2$ (In fact $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p}\varepsilon_{q}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{2pq}} \in K$). As   Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}  implies that $h_2(2pq)=2$ and $h_2(2p)\geq 4$, we  deduce that $h_2(K)\geq 4$.



To complete our proof let us consider that last sub-case, i.e., $d'=q'$ is a prime number such that $q'\equiv3\pmod8$. In this sub-case we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_q,\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{2q'}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}\varepsilon_{2qq'}}\rangle}$ (cf. Table \ref{tab7}) and $h_2(2qq')=2$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}), which gives $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the form $D)$.

Hence, putting all of the above together, we obtain the complete classification stated in the theorem. This completes the proof.

body_md:
\label{class2qrs} Let $q\equiv3\pmod4$ be a prime number and $d$ a positive square-free integer. Put  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q},\sqrt{d})$. Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if, $d$ is in  one of the following forms: 
\begin{enumerate}[$A)$]
	\item $d=r,$ where $r$ is a prime number such that we have one of the following conditions:
	\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
		\item $r\equiv3\pmod4$ and  $[ q\equiv3\pmod 8  \text{ or }   r\equiv3\pmod 8 ]$, 
		\item $r\equiv1\pmod4$ and $h_2(2qr)=4.$ 
	\end{enumerate}  
	\item $d=rs$, where $r$ and $s$ are prime numbers such that, after a suitable permutation of $r$ and $s$, we have one of the following conditions:
	
	\begin{enumerate}[\rm $1)$]
		
		\item $q\equiv s\equiv7\pmod{8}$, $r\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
		
		
		
		\item $r\equiv s\equiv3\pmod{8}$, $q\equiv7\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$,
		                            
		\item $r\equiv5\pmod8$, $s\equiv1\pmod{8}$, $q\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
		
		
		
		
		\item $r\equiv s\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$,
		\item $r\equiv1\pmod8, s\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)=\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=-1$.
		
		
		
		
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\item $d=2p,$   where $p\equiv1\pmod4$  prime number such that we have one of the following conditions:
	\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
		\item $p\equiv5\pmod8$,
		\item $p\equiv1\pmod8$,  $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	\item $d=2pq_1,$   where $p\equiv-q_1\equiv1\pmod4$ and $q_1\neq q$  are two prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
		\item $p\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\dfrac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\dfrac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)=1]$,
		
		\item $p\equiv1\pmod8$ and  $\left(\dfrac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{p}{q}\right)=-1$. 
	\end{enumerate} 
	                                                                                                                                                                                                         
	                                                               
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
Notice that if $h_2(K)=2$, then by Kuroda's class number formula     and Lemma \ref{realQuadodd}, we deduce that $h_2(2qd)\leq 8$; and so  by genus theory we conclude that $d$ has at most  {three} distinct prime divisors. So we  have the following cases to investigate:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item Let $d=r$ be a prime number that is co-prime with $2q$. Assume that $h_2(K)=2$. If $r\equiv3\pmod4$, the quadratic extension  $K/\mathbb{Q}(2qr)$ is  ramified, and so    $h_2(2qr)=1$ or $2$. As there is no real quadratic field of this form that has an odd class number (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadodd}), we have $h_2(2qr)=2$,  which is equivalent to $q$ or $r \equiv3\pmod8$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}). Conversely, if $r\equiv3\pmod 4$ and $q$ or $r \equiv3\pmod8$, then by using Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo}),   we check that $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_r, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{r}\varepsilon_{2q}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{2qr}}\rangle}$ (cf. Table \ref{tab7} and Lemma \ref{unitsrs}), i.e., $q(K)=4$. It follows, by  Kuroda's class number formula,   that $h_2(K)=2$.
	
	Now if $r\equiv1\pmod4$, then $K/\mathbb{Q}(2qr)$ is an unramified quadratic extension. Therefore $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if  $h_2(2qr)=4$. This justifies the form $A)$. 
	\item  Let $d=rs$ for some distinct prime numbers $r$ and $s$ coprime with $2q$. 
	Put $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2qrs})$ and assume that  $h_2(K)=2$. Notice  that if $K/k$ is ramified, then $h_2(k)\in \{1,2\}$, which is impossible  according to  Lemmas \ref{realQuadodd} and \ref{realQuadeven1New}. Therefore,
	$K/k$ is unramified, and so  necessarily $rs\equiv1\pmod4$. Yields that we have two cases to investigate:
	
	\noindent\ding{229}  Assume that  $r\equiv s\equiv 3\pmod4$. According to \cite[Theorem 1]{BS95} we have $k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}$, and so 
	$	h_2(K)=\frac{h_2(k)}{2}$. Therefore,    
	$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $h_2(k)=4$.
	On the other hand, the quadratic fields $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2qrs})$ such that $h_2(k)=4$ can be deduced from  \cite[Form $c_i$, for $i\in \{1,...,3\}$,  page 11]{BS25I}. In fact, we have $h_2(k)=4$ if and only if, after a suitable permutation of  $q, r$ and $s$, we have $r\equiv3\pmod8$,  $q\equiv7\pmod8$,   $\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)=1$ and one of the   conditions in Table \ref{table5}.
	
	{\footnotesize	\begin{center}
			\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
			\begin{table}[H]
				\begin{tabular}{c|c|cc}
					\toprule
					Cas
					
					& $s \pmod{8}$
					&  $\left(\dfrac{q}{r}\right)$&  $\left(\dfrac{q}{s}\right)$ \\
					\midrule
					$c_{1}$ & $7$ & $1$& $-1$ \\
					$c_{2}$ & $7$ & $1$& $1$ \\
					$c_{3}$ & $3$ & $-1$& $1$ \\
					\bottomrule
				\end{tabular}
				\caption{Conditions on $r$, $s$ and $q$ ensuring $h_2(2qrs)=4$ in  case  $r\equiv s\equiv3\pmod4$}\label{table5}
			\end{table}
	\end{center}}
	
	
	\noindent\ding{229} Now assume that  $r\equiv s \equiv 1\pmod4$. Under the hypothesis $h_2(K)=2$, the 2-class field tower of $k$ is abelian,  i.e.,  $k^{(1)}= k^{(2)}$. Hence,  using the classification in \cite[Form $c_i$, for $i\in \{19,...,22,25,26\}$, page 176]{BS95}, by interpreting the graphs corresponding to the abelian case to those of type 6, we have : 
	
	
	{	\begin{center}
			\footnotesize
			\begin{table}[H]
				\renewcommand{1.3}{1.4}
				\begin{tabular}{c|ccc|ccc}
					\toprule
					Cas
					& $r \pmod{8}$
					& $s \pmod{8}$
					& $q \pmod{8}$ & $\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)$
					& $\left(\dfrac{r}{q}\right)$ &  $\left(\dfrac{s}{q}\right)$ \\
					\midrule
					$c_{19}$ & $5$ & $1$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $1$ & $1$ \\
					$c_{20}$ & $5$ & $1$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $1$&$-1$  \\
					$c_{21}$ & $5$ & $5$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $1$ &$-1$ \\
					$c_{22}$ & $5$ & $5$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $1$  &$-1$\\
					$c_{25}$ & $1$ & $5$ & $7$ & $-1$ & $-1$  &$-1$\\
					$c_{26}$ & $1$ & $5$ & $3$ & $-1$ & $-1$  &$-1$ \\
					\bottomrule
				\end{tabular}
				\caption{Conditions on $r$, $s$ and $q$ ensuring $h_2(2qrs)=4$ in abelian case and $r\equiv s\equiv1\pmod4$}\label{abelien2qrs}
			\end{table}
	\end{center}}
	
	
	
	
	Conversely, every row of Table \ref{abelien2qrs} guarantees that \(h_2(k)=4\). 
	Hence, to obtain \(h_2(K)=2\), it remains to verify that \(k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}\). 
	Therefore, by \cite[Theorem 2]{BLS98}, apart from the case \(c_{19}\), 
	the 2-class tower of \(k\) is abelian in all the remaining cases.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	This justifies the form $B)$.
	\item Let $d=rst$, where $r$, $s$ and $t$ are distinct prime numbers co-prime with $2q$. By genus theory, we obtain $h_2(rst)\geq 2$ and $h_2(2qrst)\geq 8$. It follows that  $h_2(K)\geq 4$, which forces the rejection of this case.
	
	\item Let $d=2d'$, for an odd positive integer $d'$ coprime with $q$. Assume that $h_2(K)=2$. As $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qd'})$ and $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2d'})$ ramifies, we have 
	$h_2(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{qd'})), h_2(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2d'})) \in \{1,2\}\}$. It follows,  by Lemmas \ref{realQuadodd} and \ref{realQuadeven1New}, that we have:
	\[
	d' = \begin{cases}
		1, \;\text{ or }  \\
		q_1,  \text{ with }  q_1\equiv3\pmod 4,  \text{ or } \\
		p,  \text{ with }  p\equiv5\pmod 8  \text{ or } [  p\equiv1\pmod 8 \text{ and } \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1 ],  \text{ or } \\
		q_1p,   \text{ with }  \left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1   \text{ or }   [ p\equiv5\pmod8  \text{ and }  \left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1].
	\end{cases}
	\]
	
	Where $p\equiv-q_1\equiv1\pmod4$ distinct prime numbers.
	For the 	converse, if  $d'=1$  then $h_2(K)=1$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realBiquad}) and so this case is rejected. 
	Moreover, if  $d'=q_1$ for a prime number $q_1\equiv3\pmod4$ distinct to $q$, then according to Lemma \ref{realQuadodd} and Kuroda's class number formula, we have $h_2(K)=q(K)/4$ and  making use of  Table \ref{tab7} and    Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo}),  we check that  $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{2q_1}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{qq_1}}\rangle}$, this gives $h_2(K)=1$. So the second case is also rejected.
	
	Now let $d'$ takes the third form,  i.e., $d'=p$, such that  $p\equiv5\pmod 8$  \text{ or } $[  p\equiv1\pmod 8 \text{ and } \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1 ]$. By Kuroda's class number formula and Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}, we have : $h_2(K)=\frac{q(K)h_2(2p)h_2(pq)}{4}=q(K).$
	Moreover, by making	use of Table \ref{tab7} and Lemma \ref{unitsrs}, we check that if $p\equiv5\pmod8$ then  $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q},\varepsilon_{2p},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{pq}} \;\text{or}\; \sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq}}\rangle}$ according to whether $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=1$ or not, thus $h_2(K)=2$. But if  $  p\equiv1\pmod 8 \text{ and } \left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$, we check that $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q},\varepsilon_{2p},  \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{2p}} \rangle}$ (notice that accordint to \cite[Theorem 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p})=1$). Therefore  $h_2(K)=2$.
	This justifies the form $C)$. 
	
	
	
	Finally let $d'=q_1p$, with  $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1   \text{ or }   [ p\equiv5\pmod8  \text{ and }  \left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1]$. Then $h_2(K)=\frac{q(K)h_2(2pq_1)h_2(pqq_1)}{4}=q(K).$ We begin by the first case where $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1,$ then if $p\equiv1\pmod8$ we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q },\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{2pq_1}}, \varepsilon_{pqq_1}\; \text{or}\; \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{pqq_1}} \rangle}$ according to whether $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$ or not. But if $p\equiv5\pmod8$ we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q },\varepsilon_{2pq_1},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}\varepsilon_{pqq_1}}\; \text{or}\; \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pq_1}\varepsilon_{pqq_1}} \rangle}$ according to whether $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=1$ or not  (cf. Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8}). Therefore, if $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1$, we have $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or $[p\equiv1\pmod8 \;\text{and}\; \left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1]$. At the end if $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=1$, $p\equiv5\pmod8  \text{ and }  \left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$, we check that $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q },\varepsilon_{2pq_1}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pq_1}\varepsilon_{pqq_1}} \rangle}$ (cf. Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8}), then $h_2(K)=2$.  This justifies the form $D)$. 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	\item Now let $d=qd'$ for an odd positive integer $d'$ co-prime with $q$. Then \(K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q},\sqrt{qd'})=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q},\sqrt{2d'})\), and this case has already been treated in the preceding case.
	
	
	                                                                                                                                                                                                       
	                    
		                       
			                         
			                                                            
			                                                                                                                                                                
			                                                                                                                      
			                
		        
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
	     
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
	       
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
	        
	                        
		                                                                                                                                          
		                                                                                                                                                                                    
		                                                                                                                                                                                                  
		                
	        
	                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
\end{enumerate}
Plugging  all of the above investigations together, we   complete the proof of our classification.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{classq1q2d}
Let $q_1\equiv q_2 \equiv3\pmod4$ be distinct prime numbers and   $d$ a positive square-free integer. Put $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2},\sqrt{d})$.	Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $d$ is in one of the following forms : 
\begin{enumerate}[$A)$]
\item $d=2,$ such that $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv7\pmod8$ and  $h_2(2q_1q_2)=4.$
\item $d=p,$ where $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is a prime number such that     $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1 $ and $h_2(pq_1q_2)=4$.
\item $d=2p,$ where $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is a prime  number such that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8,q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1,$ or
	
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8,q_1\equiv7\pmod8, q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_2}{q_1}\right)=-1.$
\end{enumerate}

\item $d=q_3,$ where $q_3\equiv3\pmod4$ is a prime number such that  one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $q_1\equiv q_3 \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=1$,
	                         
	\item  $q_1\equiv q_2 \equiv 3\pmod{8}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=1$,
	
	                         
	
	\item  $q_2\equiv7\pmod8$, $q_3 \equiv 3\pmod{8}$, $q_1\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$,
	
	                         
	
	\item $q_2\equiv3\pmod8$, $q_3 \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $q_1\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$.
	
	                         
	
\end{enumerate}
\item $d=2q_3,$ where $q_3\equiv3\pmod4$ is a prime number such that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $q_3\equiv q_2\equiv7\pmod{8}$, $q_1\equiv3\pmod{8}$, and
	$\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=1$.
	
	
	
	\item $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod{8}$, $q_3\equiv7\pmod{8}$, and
	$\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_3}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$.
\end{enumerate}
\item $d=p_1p_2,$ where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1,$
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1.$
\end{enumerate}
\item $d=q_3q_4,$ where $q_3\equiv q_4\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_4}\right)=\left(\frac{q_4}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_1}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_4}\right)=1,$ or
	\item $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_4}\right)=\left(\frac{q_4}{q_3}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_4}\right)=1.$
\end{enumerate}
\item $d=2q_1q_3,$ where $q_3\equiv3\pmod8$ is a prime number coprime with $q_1q_2$.
\item $d=pq_1,$ where $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is a prime number such that $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1$.
\item $d=2pq_1,$  where $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is a prime number such that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1,$ 
	\item $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1$ and $p\equiv5\pmod8.$
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d$ be a positive square-free integer. We have two main cases to investigate.


\noindent\ding{229} Assume that $\mathrm{gcd}(d,q_1q_2)=1$.  Put $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2d})$.  We note that $K/k$ is an unramified quadratic extension. So by Remark \ref{abelianquaexten}, we have 
$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $h_2(k)=4$ and $k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}$. In particular, 
if $h_2(K)=2$, then the $2$-class group of $k$  is cyclic or it is the Klein $4$-group; and so by genus theory, we have one of the following forms for $d$:   
\begin{center}
[$d=2$ or $d=p$]   or 	[$d= q_3 $, $d= 2q_3 $, $d= 2p$, $d= p_1p_2 $ or $d= q_3q_4$], 
\end{center}
where $p\equiv p_i\equiv -q_i\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Now let us explore each form.
\begin{enumerate}[\noindent$i)$]
\item Let $d=2$ (resp.  $d=p$). Since $A(k)$ is cyclic, 
we deduce from class field theory and Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New} that $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if
$q_1\equiv q_2\equiv 7\pmod 8$ and  $h(2q_1q_2)=4$ (resp.     $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1 $ and $h_2(pq_1q_2)=4$). This justifies the forms $A)$ and $B)$ respectively.


\item Let $d=2p$. Since $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ ramify, this implies that $h_2(2p) = 2$, and thus $p\equiv5\pmod8$ (cf. Lemmas \ref{realQuadeven1New} and \ref{realQuadodd}). According to \cite[page 175, cases $c_{12}-c_{14}$]{BS95}, we have    $k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}$  and $h_2(k)=4$  if  and only if one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8,q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1,$ or
	
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8,q_1\equiv7\pmod8, q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_2}{q_1}\right)=-1.$
\end{enumerate}
This justifies the form $C)$.
\item Let $d=q_3$. By Theorem \ref{classqrs}, $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if we have one of the conditions listed in $D)$.  
\item Let $d=2q_3.$  By Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New},  $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if we have one of the conditions listed in $E)$.  
\item Let $d=p_1p_2.$   According to \cite[page 175, cases $c_{12}-c_{14}$]{BS95} we have $h_2(p_1p_2q_1q_2)=4$ and $k^{(1)}=k^{(2)}$  if and only if we have one of the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1,$
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1.$
\end{enumerate}
This justifies the form $F)$.
\item Let $d=q_3q_4.$ We note that according \cite[Theorem 1]{BS95} the $2$-class field of $k$ is abelian. Moreover,  using \cite[page 11, $c_1-c_3$]{BS25I} we deduce that $h_2(q_1q_2q_3q_4)=4$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:  
\begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_4}\right)=\left(\frac{q_4}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_1}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_4}\right)=1,$ or
	\item $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_4}\right)=\left(\frac{q_4}{q_3}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_4}\right)=1.$
\end{enumerate}
This justifies the form $G)$.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent\ding{229} Now assume that $\mathrm{gcd}(d,q_1q_2)=q_1$.    Put $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_2d'})$, where $d'=\frac {d}{q_1}$. As $K/k$ ramify, the equality $h_2(K)=2$ implies that $h_2(k)\in\{1,2\}$; and thus  Lemmas  \ref{realQuadodd} and \ref{realQuadeven1New} imply that: 
\[
d'\in \{1,2,q,2q_3,p,2p\},
\]
where $q\equiv q_3\equiv -p\equiv3\pmod4$ are  prime numbers satisfying some extra conditions as below. For the converse,
let us explore these forms of $d'$. Firstly, notice that the forms $d'=1$, $2$ and $q$ are eliminated. In fact,  each of these cases gives $h_2(K)=1$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realBiquad}). Now let us investigate each of the remaining forms.
\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
\item $d'=2q_3,$ for some prime number $q_3\equiv3\pmod8$ distinct from $q_1$ and $q_2$. Using Table \ref{tab7} and  Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo})  we conclude that  $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{2q_1q_3},\eta\rangle}$, where $$\eta \in \{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q_1q_3}\varepsilon_{2q_2q_3}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2q_2q_3}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2q_2q_3}\varepsilon_{2q_1q_3}}\}.$$  Therefore $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the form $H)$. 
\item Let $d'=p,$ for some prime number $p\equiv1\pmod4$ such that $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1$. From Table \ref{tab7} we get $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{pq_1}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq_1}\varepsilon_{pq_2}}\;or\;\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq_1}\varepsilon_{pq_2}\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}}\rangle}$. So by Kuroda's class number formula and Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}, we have $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the form $I)$. 
\item Now let $d'=2p,$ for some prime number $p\equiv1\pmod4$ such that $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1$. Notice that $q(K)=4$ or $2$ according to whether  $p\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1$ or not. In fact using Table \ref{tab7} and  Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo}) we check that:

\begin{center}
	\begin{table}[H]
		\begin{tabular}{c|cc|c}
			\toprule
			$p\pmod8$ & $\left(\dfrac{p}{q_1}\right)$ & $ \left(\dfrac{p}{q_2}\right)$ & $E_K$ \\
			\toprule
			$5$	&  $1$&$1$ &  $\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pq_1}\varepsilon_{2pq_2}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2pq_1}}\rangle}$ \\
			\midrule
			$5$	&  $-1$&$-1$ &  $\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{2pq_1},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pq_1}\varepsilon_{2pq_2}}\rangle}$ \\
			
			\midrule
			$5$	&  $1$&$-1$ &  $\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{2pq_2},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2pq_1}}\rangle}$  \\
			
			\midrule
			$1$	&  $-1$&$-1$ &  $\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{2pq_1},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pq_1}\varepsilon_{2pq_2}}\rangle}$ \\
			
			
			\bottomrule
		\end{tabular}
		\caption{Unit group of $K$ when $d=2pq_1$}
	\end{table}
\end{center}
Therefore by applying Kuroda's class number formula and Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}, we deduce that $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if \begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1,$  or
	\item $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1$ and $p\equiv5\pmod8.$
\end{enumerate}
This justifies the form $J)$.  		This completes the proof of our theorem.
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{class2d}
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{d})$, where  $d$ is an odd  positive square-free integer. 
Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if, $d$ is in  one of the following forms: 
\begin{enumerate}[$A)$]
\item $d=pq,$ where $p\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are prime numbers such that  $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1.$
\item $d=p,$ where $p$ is a prime number such that $p\equiv1\pmod8$, $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{8}}$ and $h_2(2p)=4.$
\item $d=q_1q_2,$ where $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv7\pmod8$ are distinct prime numbers such that  $h_2(2q_1q_2)=4.$
\item $d=p_1p_2$, where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers satisfying one of the following conditions:

\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$, $h(2p_1p_2)=4$ and \textbf{none} of the two units $\{\varepsilon_{2}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}, \varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}\}$ is a square in $K$,
	\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$,
	$h(2p_1p_2)=4$ and \textbf{none} of the two units $\{ \varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}, \varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}\}$ is a square in $K$.
\end{enumerate} 


                                                                                                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                         
\item $d=pq_1q_2,$ where $p\equiv-q_1\equiv-q_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that, after a suitable permutation of $q_1$ and $q_2$, we have one of the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8$, $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=1,$
	\item $p\equiv5\pmod8$, $q_1\equiv 7\pmod8$, $q_2\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{q_2}{q_1}\right)=1.$
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{d})$, with $d$   an odd positive square-free integer.                                                                                                                             
Our proof consists of two parts, according to the equivalence class of $d  \pmod4$. 

\noindent\ding{229} Assume that $d\equiv3\pmod4$. So $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2d})$ ramify and thus  the conditions $h_2(K)=2$, implies that we have   $h_2(2d)=1$ or $2$. 
Conversely, notice that if $h_2(2d) =1$,   then $d=q\equiv3\pmod4$ is a prime number (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadodd}); and  this implies that the class number of $K$ is odd (cf. Lemma \ref{realBiquad}). So this case eliminated.

Now let $h_2(2d)=2$. So Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}  implies that  $d=pq$,  where  $p\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are prime numbers such that $p\equiv5\pmod8$ or  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1.$ 
Thus, we have $h(pq)=h(2pq)=2$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}) and  $q(K)=2$  (In fact $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{pq}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq}\varepsilon_{2pq}}\rangle}$   by Wada's algorithm and Table \ref{tab7}). Consequently, Kuroda's class number formula gives $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the form $A)$.

\noindent\ding{229} Now assume that $d\equiv1\pmod4$. Thus, $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2d})$ is an unramified quadratic extension.   Notice that if  $h_2(K)=2$, then  $h_2(2d)= 4$    and so $h_2(d)q(K)=2$. This implies that $h_2(d)=1$ or $2$. So we have two sub-cases to investigate.                             
\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
\item Assume that 	$h_2(d)=1$.  So, by Lemma \ref{realQuadodd}, we have $d=p$, where $p \equiv1\pmod4$ is a prime number, or $d=q_1q_2$, where $ q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Moreover, we have:
\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
	\item If $d=p$,  then   \cite[Theorem 2]{kuvcera1995parity}  implies that, $p\equiv1\pmod 8$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{8}}$.  Therefore, by class field theory,
	$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if  $h_2(2p)=4$.  This justifies the form $B)$.
	\item Now if $d=q_1q_2$, then, by class field theory and  Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New},  $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv7\pmod8$ and $h_2(2q_1q_2)=4$. This justifies the form $C)$.
\end{enumerate}





\item Assume that $h_2(d)=2$. By Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}, we have one of the following   cases:
    
                   
	                                                                                                                                   
	                                                                                                                                                                                                            
	                                                                                                                                                          
	            
	    
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item 	If $d$ takes the   first form, i.e., $d=p_1p_2$ $\text{ with }  p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod 4  \text{ and }  \left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$, then according to \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$ and   using  \cite[Theorem 2.2]{AzZektaous} we deduce  that  
		$q(K)=2$ or $1$, according to whether one of the units $\{ {\varepsilon_{2}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}} ,   {\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}}\}$ is a square in $K$ or not. 
		
		Since by Kuroda's class number formula, we have $h_2(K)=\frac12 q(K)h_2(2p_1p_2)$, we deduce that 
		$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $q(K)=1$  and  $h_2(2p_1p_2)=4$. This justifies the form $D)-1)$.  
		
		
		\item Now if  $d$ takes  the second form, i.e.,   $d=p_1p_2$ $\text{ with }  p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod 4  \text{ and }   [\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4]$, then according to \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$ and   using  \cite[Theorem 2.2]{AzZektaous} we deduce  that  
		$q(K)=2$ or $1$, according to whether one of the units	$\{ {\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}} ,   {\varepsilon_{2p_1p_2}}\}$ is a square in $K$ or not.
		Thus,	Kuroda's class number formula gives $h_2(K)=\frac12 q(K)h_2(2p_1p_2)$. Therefore,
		$h_2(K)=2$ if and only if $q(K)=1$  and  $h_2(2p_1p_2)=4$. This justifies the form $D)-2)$.  
		
		
		\item  Now if  $d$ takes  the third form, i.e., $d=pq_1q_2$ with $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv-p\equiv3\pmod 4$ and  $(\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1)$, then  according to \cite[  Page 175 : $c_{12}-c_{14}$]{BS95}, we have  Table \ref{2dabelien} that characterizes when do we have exactly $h(2pq_1q_2)=4$. 
		{\footnotesize	\begin{center}
				\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
				\begin{table}[H]
					\begin{tabular}{c|ccc|ccc}
						\toprule
						Case
						& $p \pmod{8}$
						& $q_1 \pmod{8}$
						& $q_2 \pmod{8}$ & $\left(\dfrac{q_2}{p}\right)$
						& $\left(\dfrac{q_2}{q_1}\right)$ &  $\left(\dfrac{p}{q_1}\right)$ \\
						\midrule
						
						$c_{12}$ & $5$ & $3$ & $3$ & $1$ & $-1$  &$-1$\\
						$c_{13}$ & $5$ & $3$ & $3$ & $1$ & $1$  &$-1$\\
						$c_{14}$ & $5$ & $7$ & $3$ & $1$ & $-1$  &$-1$ \\
						\bottomrule
					\end{tabular}
					\caption{Conditions on $p$, $q_1$ and $q_2$ ensuring $h_2(2pq_1q_2)=4$ in abelian $2$-tower case where $p\equiv -q_1\equiv-q_2\equiv1\pmod4$}\label{2dabelien}\label{abelien2pq1q2}
				\end{table}
		\end{center}}
		On the other hand, assuming that $d=2pq_1q_2$, where $p$, $q_1$ and $q_2$ are prime numbers satisfying one of   the conditions in  Table \ref{abelien2pq1q2}, we make use of Table  \ref{tab8} and Wada's method to check that we have $q(K)=1$. Thus under each of these conditions we have $h_2(K)=2$.  This justifies the form $E)$. 	
	\end{enumerate}
	Combining all of the above investigations,   we complete  the proof of our classification in the above theorem.	
	\end{enumerate}

body_md:
As \(N(\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}) = N(\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}) = 1\) and \(N(\varepsilon_p) = -1\)  we need to determine the   the forms of:
$$\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}, \;\;\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}  \text{ and }  \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}.$$
Here we give the proof of the first item in details, and the prove of the second item is analogous. Let us assume that 
$\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1.$ So we have three main cases to investigate:
 
	
	\noindent\ding{229} Assume that $x,y, a$ and $b$ are integers.  Then $x^2-p_1q_1q_2y^2=a^2-pp_1q_1q_2b^2=1$. Then by  taking into account the unique factorization in $\mathbb{Z}$ and using Lemma \ref{ZekTAo} we have one of the following systems: 
 	$$(1):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		x\pm 1=2p_1y_1^2\\
		x\mp 1=2q_1q_2 y_2^2,
	\end{array}\right. \quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(2):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		x\pm 1=2q_1y_1^2\\
		x\mp 1=2p_1q_2 y_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(3):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		x\pm 1=2q_2y_1^2\\
		x\mp 1=2p_1q_1 y_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	$$	
	where $y_1$ and $y_2$ are two integers such that  $y=2y_1 y_2$.
	
	\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
		\item The first system can not occur, since it implies that :
		$$\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\mp 2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{x\pm1\mp 2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{x\mp1}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{2q_1q_2}{p_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right).$$ 
		\item Similarly the second system implies that: 
		$$\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\pm 2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{x\mp1\pm 2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{x\pm1}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{2q_1}{p_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right).$$ 
		
	\end{enumerate}
	From the third system we get $2q_2(x+1)$ or $2q_2(x-1)$ is a square in $\mathbb{N}$ according to whether $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$ or not. Then $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}=y_1\sqrt{q_2}+y_2\sqrt{p_1q_1}$. Similarly we have  the following possible systems :
	
	$$(1):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		a\pm 1=2pp_1b_1^2\\
		a\mp 1=2q_1q_2 b_2^2,
	\end{array}\right. \quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(2):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		a\pm 1=2pq_1b_1^2\\
		a\mp 1=2p_1q_2 b_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(3):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		a\pm 1=2pq_2b_1^2\\
		a\mp 1=2p_1q_1 b_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	$$	
	where $b_1$ and $b_2$ are two integers such that  $b=2b_1 b_2$.
	
	\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
		\item The first system implies that: 
		$$\left(\frac{2}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{a+1 }{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{a-1+ 2}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{2pp_1}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{2}{q_2}\right), \;\;\text{or}$$ 
		
		$$\left(\frac{-2}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{a-1 }{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{a+1- 2}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{2pp_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{2}{q_1}\right)$$
		which is a contradiction.
		\item By the same way we prove that the third system can bot occur. Finally it remains the second system and from which we get $2pq_1(x+1)$ or $2pq_1(x-1)$ is square according to whether $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$ or not. Therefore  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}=b_1\sqrt{pq_1}+b_2\sqrt{p_1q_2}$. Then by using Wada's algorithm we conclude that  $q(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{p_1q_1q_2}))=1$.
		
	\end{enumerate}
	\noindent\ding{229} Now we assume that  $x$ and $y$ are integers, $a$ and $b$ are semi integers such that  $a=\alpha/2$ and $b=\beta/2$ for some integers $\alpha$  and $\beta$. According to the previous case we have $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}=y_1\sqrt{q_2}+y_2\sqrt{p_1q_1}$. For the second square we proceed as before. Then from $\alpha^2-4=pp_1q_1q_2\beta^2$ and according to Lemma \ref{ZekTAo} we have the following possible systems: 
		{\footnotesize	\begin{center}
			\renewcommand{1.3}{1.6}
			\begin{table}[H]
				\begin{tabular}{cccc}
					 $(1):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
						\alpha\pm 2=p\beta_1^2\\
						\alpha\mp 2=p_1q_1q_2 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right. $
					& $(2):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
						\alpha\pm 2=p_1\beta_1^2\\
						\alpha\mp 2=pq_1q_2 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right. $
					& $(3):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
						\alpha\pm 2=q_1\beta_1^2\\
						\alpha\mp 2=pp_1q_2 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right. $ & $(4):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
					\alpha\pm 2=q_2\beta_1^2\\
					\alpha\mp 2=pp_1q_1 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right. $\\
				
					
					$(5):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
						\alpha\pm 2=pp_1\beta_1^2\\
						\alpha\mp 2=q_1q_2 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right. $& $(6):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
					\alpha\pm 2=pq_1\beta_1^2\\
					\alpha\mp 2=p_1q_2 \beta_2^2,
					\end{array}\right.$& $(7):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
					\alpha\pm 2=pq_2\beta_1^2\\
					\alpha\mp 2=p_1q_1\beta_2^2.
					\end{array}\right.$& 
					
				
				\end{tabular}
				
			\end{table}
	\end{center}}
	where $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are integers such that $\beta=\beta_1\beta_2$.
	\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
		\item The first system can not occur since it implies: 
		
		
		$$1=\left(\frac{\pm4}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\mp2\pm4}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\pm2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=-1.$$
		\item Similarly for the second system:
		$$1=\left(\frac{\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\mp2\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\pm2}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p}\right)=-1.$$
		
		\item Similarly for the third system:
		$$1=\left(\frac{\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\mp2\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\pm2}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{p}\right)=-1.$$
		\item Similarly for the fourth system:
		$$1=\left(\frac{\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\mp2\pm4}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\pm2}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{q_2}{p}\right)=-1.$$
		
		
		\item Similarly for the fifth system:
		$$1=\left(\frac{4}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha-2+4}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha+2}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{pp_1}{q_2}\right)=-1,\;\text{or}$$
		$$-1=\left(\frac{-4}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha+2-4}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha-2}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{pp_1}{q_1}\right)=1.$$
		
		
		\item The same thing for the seventh system:
		
		$$1=\left(\frac{\pm4}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\mp2\pm4}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\alpha\pm2}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{pq_2}{p_1}\right)=-1.$$
		
	\end{enumerate}
	Then it remains the sixth system which implies that $pq_1(x+2)$ or $pq_1(x-2)$ is a square in $\mathbb{N}$ according to whether   $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$ or not. Therefore $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}=\frac{1}{2}(\beta_1\sqrt{pq_1}+\beta_2\sqrt{p_1q_2})$ and so  $q(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{p_1q_1q_2}))=1$.
	
	
	
	
	\noindent\ding{229} Now if that  $x$, $y$, $a$ and $b$ are semi-integers. Then $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}=\frac{1}{4}(\beta_1\sqrt{pq_1}+\beta_2\sqrt{p_1q_2})$. Moreover we have $z^2-4=t^2p_1q_1q_2$, where $z$ and $t$ are integers such that $x=z/2$ and $y=t/2$, then Lemma \ref{ZekTAo} implies the following possible systems:
	
	
	$$(1):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		z\pm 2=p_1t_1^2\\
		z\mp 2=q_1q_2 t_2^2,
	\end{array}\right. \quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(2):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		z\pm 2=q_1t_1^2\\
		z\mp 2=p_1q_2 t_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	\text{or}\quad
	(3):\ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
		z\pm 2=q_2t_1^2\\
		z\mp 2=p_1q_1 t_2^2,
	\end{array}\right.\quad
	$$	
	where $t_1$ and $t_2$ are two integers such that  $t=t_1 t_2$. Using the same argument as in the previous two cases we check that $q_2(x+2)$ or $q_2(x-2)$ is square in $\mathbb{N}$ according to whether $\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$ or not. Thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}=\frac{1}{2}(t_1\sqrt{q_2}+t_2\sqrt{p_1q_1})$ and $q(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{p_1q_1q_2}))=1$.
	
	
	
	
	\noindent\ding{229} Finally if   $x$ and $y$ are semi integers, a and b are integers. Then from the previous sub-cases we have $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}=\frac{1}{2}(t_1\sqrt{q_2}+t_2\sqrt{p_1q_1})$  and  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pp_1q_1q_2}}=b_1\sqrt{pq_1}+b_2\sqrt{p_1q_2}$. Then  $q(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{p_1q_1q_2}))=1$.
 
This completes the proof.

\label{classpd}
Let  $p\equiv1\pmod4$ be a prime number and   $d$ a  positive square-free integer co-prime with $p$. Put $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{d})$.	Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if, $d$ is in one of the following forms: 
\begin{enumerate}[$A)$]
	\item $d=2$, with $p\equiv1\pmod8$, $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{8}}$ and $h_2(2p)=4.$
	\item $d=p_1,$ with $p_1\equiv1\pmod4$ a prime number such that $h_2(pp_1)=4.$
	
	\item $d=\eta q,$ where $\eta\in \{1,2\}$ and $q\equiv3\pmod4$ is a prime number such that $p\equiv1\pmod8$,  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=1$ and  $h_2(\eta pq)=4$.
	
	\item $d=q_1q_2$, where $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv
	3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers  such that  $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1$ and $h_2(pq_1q_2)=4.$
	\item $d=p_1q$, where $p_1\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that $p_1\equiv5\pmod8$ and one of the following conditions holds: 
	\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
		\item $p\equiv1\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1,$
		                                                                                                                               
		\item $p\equiv1\pmod8, q\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1,$
		
		\item $p\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1.$ 
	\end{enumerate}
	\item $d=2p_1q$ with $p_1\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers satisfying one of the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}[$1)$]

	\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]

		\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1, \left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$, $h_2(pp_1p_2)=4$ and \textbf{none} of the  units  $\{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2},\varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}, \varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}\}$  is a square in $K$.
	\end{enumerate} 
	
	
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
Let $d$ be a positive square-free integer co-prime with $p$. Notice that the extension  $K/k$, with $k=\mathbb{Q}(pd)$, is an unramified quadratic extension. Assume that  $h_2(K)=2$. Then $h_2(pd)=4$ and by   Kuroda's class number formula, we deduce that   
$h_2(d)=1$ (in this case $q(K)=2$) or $h_2(d)=2$ (in this case $q(K)=1$). So we have two main cases to investigate.

\noindent\ding{229}	  Assume that $ h_2(d)=1$. By Lemma \ref{realQuadodd}, $d\in \{2,p_1,q,2q, q_1q_2\}$, where $p_1\equiv-q\equiv-q_1\equiv-q_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. In particular, we have:
\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
	\item Letting $d=2$, then as in the proof of Theorem \ref{class2d}, we deduce that $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if 
	$p\equiv1\pmod8$, $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{8}}$ and $h_2(2p)=4$.   This justifies the form $A)$.
	\item Letting $d=p_1$, with $p_1\equiv1\pmod4$   a prime number.   Thus, by class field theory,  $h_2(K)=2$ exactly when $h_2(pp_1)=4$. This justifies the form $B)$.
	\item Letting  $d=\eta q$ with $q\equiv3\pmod4$ prime number, we deduce from the condition
	$h_2(\eta pq)=4$ that we have  $p\equiv1\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=1$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}).
	Thus, in this case,   by class field theory  $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if  $p\equiv1\pmod8$,  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=1$ and $h_2(\eta pq)=4$.
	This justifies the form $C)$.
	
	\item $d=q_1q_2$ where $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Notice that the condition $h_2(pq_1q_2)=4$ implies that  $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=1$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}). So by class field theory  we have   $h_2(K)=2$ if and only of $h_2(pq_1q_2)=4$. This justifies the form $D)$.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent\ding{229}	  Now assume that $ h_2(d)=2$. By Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}, $d\in \{p_1q,2p_1q,2q_1q_2,p_1q_1q_2, 2p_1, p_1p_2\}$, where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv-q_1\equiv q_2 \equiv 1\pmod4$ are prime numbers that satisfy extra condition as in each case   below.   
\begin{enumerate}[$\star$]
	\item Let $d=p_1q$, where $p_1\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are  prime numbers such that  $p_1\equiv5\pmod 8$ or $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1$. Thus, 
	$h_2(pp_1q)=4$, then (by letting $p=r$ and $p_1=s$) the primes $p, p_1$ and $q$ satisfy the conditions $c_{15}-c_{20}$ in Table \ref{qrsabelien} (cf. \cite[page 177-178]{BS95}). 
	
	Conversely using Tables \ref{tab7}, \ref{tab8} and  Wada's algorithm (cf. Page \pageref{wadaalgo}) we check that $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{p},\varepsilon_{p_1q} , \varepsilon_{pp_1q}\rangle} $ for all such cases of Table \ref{qrsabelien} except the case $c_{17}$ which gives $q(K)=2$ (In fact, in this case we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{p},\varepsilon_{p_1q} , \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q}\varepsilon_{pp_1q}}\rangle} $). Hence, $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if we have one of the conditions listed from $E)$-$1)$ to $E)$-$3)$. 
	
	
	
	\item Let $d=2p_1q$, where $p_1\equiv-q\equiv1\pmod4$ are prime numbers such that $p_1\equiv5\pmod 8$ or $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1$. Notice  that if $h_2(2pp_1q)=4$, then the primes $p, p_1$ and $q$ satisfy one of the conditions $c_{19}-c_{22}$, $c_{25}- c_{26}$ in Table \ref{abelien2qrs} (cf. \cite[Page 176]{BS95}).
	Conversely by invoking Table \ref{tab8} in all previous cases except case $c_{19}$ we check that $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{p},\varepsilon_{2p_1q} , \varepsilon_{2pp_1q}\rangle} $, i.e.,   $q(K)=1$, which gives $h_2(K)=2$. For the case $c_{19}$ we get $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{p},\varepsilon_{2p_1q} , \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2pp_1q}\varepsilon_{2p_1q}}\rangle}$, then  $h_2(K)=4$ and so this case is rejected. This justifies the forms listed from $F)$-$1)$ to $F)$-$3)$.
	\item Let $d=2q_1q_2$, with $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod 4$ are distinct prime numbers such that $q_1$ or $q_2\equiv3\pmod8$.
	We note that the primes satisfying $h_2(2pq_1q_2)=4$ are exactly those satisfying one of the conditions in Table \ref{abelien2pq1q2}. Conversely, by making use of Tables \ref{tab7} and \ref{tab8} and Wada's algorithm we check that in all these  cases we have $q(K)=1$, which means that $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the forms $G)$-$1)$ and $G)$-$2)$.
	\item Let $d=p_1q_1q_2$, where $p_1\equiv-q_1\equiv-q_2\equiv1\pmod 4$ are  distinct prime numbers such that  $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$. Notice that $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pp_1q_1q_2})$ is an unramified quadratic extension. So $h_2(K)=2$ implies that  $h_2(pp_1q_1q_2)=4$.
	Moreover,  if $h_2(pp_1q_1q_2)=4$, then according to \cite[page 175, cases $c_{12}-c_{14}$]{BS95}, the primes $p$, $p_1$, $q_1$ and $q_2$ satisfy one of the following conditions: 
	\begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1,$
		\item $\left(\frac{p}{p_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{q_1}{q_2}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	Conversely, we check that if one of the   conditions  $\mathrm{C}1)$ and $\mathrm{C}2)$ holds, then making use of  Lemma \ref{unitspp1q1q2}, we check that $q(K)=1$. Since $2h_2(p_1q_1q_2)=h_2(pp_1q_1q_2)=4h_2(p)=4$, it follows that $h_2(K)=2$. This justifies the forms $H)$-$1)$ and $H)$-$2)$.
	\item Let $d=2p_1,$ where $p_1\equiv5\pmod8$ is a prime number. According to \cite[Theorem 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=-1$ and by \cite[Theorem 2.1]{AzZektaous} we check that  $q(K)=2$ or $1$ according to whether one of the units $\{\varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{2p_1}\varepsilon_{2pp_1}, \varepsilon_{2pp_1}\}$  is a square in $K$ or not. Furthermore $h_2(K)=2$ exactly when $p_1\equiv5\pmod8, h_2(2pp_1)=4$ and none of the   units $\{\varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{2p_1}\varepsilon_{2pp_1}, \varepsilon_{2pp_1}\}$ is a square in $K$. This justifies the the first item in form $I)$. 
	
	\item Let $d=2p_1,$ where $p_1\equiv1\pmod8$   is a prime number such that $\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_1}{2}\right)_4$. According to \cite[Theorem 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=1$ and by \cite[Theorem 2.1]{AzZektaous} we check that  $q(K)=2$ or $1$. according to whether $N(\varepsilon_{2pp_1})=1$ or not. Furthermore $h_2(K)=2$ exactly when $p_1\equiv1\pmod8, h_2(2pp_1)=4$, $\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_1}{2}\right)_4$ and $N(\varepsilon_{2pp_1})=-1$.  This justifies the the second item in form $I)$.
	
	
	\item Let $d=p_1p_2,$ where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod4$ distinct prime number such that $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ (cf. Lemma \ref{realQuadeven1New}). Then by \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$, thus using Wada's method we conclude that $q(K)=2$ or $1$ according to whether one of the units $\{\varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}, \varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}\}$  is a square in $K$ or not. Hence, $h_2(K)=2$ exactly when $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1, h_2(pp_1p_2)=4$ and none of the above units is a square in $K$. This justifies the first item in forms $J)$. 
	\item Let $d=p_1p_2,$ where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod4$ distinct prime number such that  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. Then by \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=1$, moreover using Wada's method we conclude that $q(K)=1$ if and only if none of the units $\{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2},\varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}, \varepsilon_{p}\varepsilon_{pp_1p_2}\}$ is a square in $K$. Hence, $h_2(K)=2$ exactly when $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1, \left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$, $h_2(pp_1p_2)=4$ and none of the above units is a square in $K$.  This justifies the second item in forms $J)$.  
\end{enumerate}This completes the proof of our result.

\label{classnoadqua}
Let $d_1$ and $d_2$ be two distinct positive  square-free integers such that  $h_2(d_1)= h_2(d_2)=h_2(d_3)=2$, where $d_3=\mathrm{sqf}(d_1d_2)$. Put $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d_1},\sqrt{d_2})$. Then $h_2(K)=2$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pq_1q_2},\sqrt{2q_1q_2})$, with $p\equiv-q_1\equiv-q_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that $p\equiv5\pmod8$, $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1$ and one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
		\item $q_1\equiv7\pmod8$ and $q_2\equiv3\pmod8$,
		\item $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3 \pmod8$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1q},\sqrt{p_2q})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2p_1q},\sqrt{2p_2q})$, with $q\equiv-p_1\equiv-p_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ and one of the following conditions holds:\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
		\item $p_1\equiv1\pmod8, p_2\equiv5\pmod8$ and  $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1,$
		\item $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate} 
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1q_1q_2},\sqrt{p_2q_1q_2})$ with $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv-p_1\equiv-p_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that after a suitable permutation of indices we have:
	$$\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1.$$
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2p_1},\sqrt{2p_2}),$ with $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers satisfying one of the following conditions:
	\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
		\item $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv5\pmod8$, 	$\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ and  $\varepsilon_{2p_1}\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}$ is not a square in $K$,
		\item $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv5\pmod8 $,  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$,
		\item $p_1\equiv5\pmod8$, $p_2\equiv1\pmod8 $,   $\left(\frac{2}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{2}\right)_4$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2},\sqrt{p_2p_3})$ with $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv p_3\equiv1\pmod4$ be distinct prime numbers satisfying one of the following conditions:
	\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=-1$ and $\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}$ is not a square in $K$,
		\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=-1$, $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=1$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_1}\right)_4$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
\end{enumerate}
