				\begin{tabular}{p{3cm}|p{3cm}|c}
					\toprule
					Form of  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq_1q_2}}$ &  Form of $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q_1q_2}}$ & Squares in $E_K$ \\
					\toprule
					$[\sqrt{q_2},\sqrt{pq_1}]$ 	&  $[\sqrt{q_2},\sqrt{2q_1}]$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{pq_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2q_1q_2}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p}\varepsilon_{2q_1q_2}}$  \\
					\cline{1-2}
					$[\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{pq_2}]$ 	&  $[\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{2q_2}]$ & $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p}\varepsilon_{pq_1q_2}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p}\varepsilon_{pq_1q_2}\varepsilon_{2q_1q_2}} $  \\
					\cline{1-2}
					$[\sqrt{p},\sqrt{q_1q_2}]$ 	&  $[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q_1q_2}]$ &   \\
					
					\bottomrule
				\end{tabular}
				\caption{The Forms of Square Roots in $E_K$}\label{formsqrt3}
			\end{table}
	\end{center}}
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	Therefore $q(K)\geq 2$, and such case must be rejected. 
	
	\item[4)-5)]  Let $(d_1,d_2)=(p_1q,p_2q)$ or $(2p_1q,p_1p_2)$ where $p_1\equiv p_2 \equiv -q \equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that  [$\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_1\equiv 5\pmod 8$], [$\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_2\equiv 5\pmod 8$] \text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$. Recalling \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity}, we have $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$. With the aid of Table \ref{tab7} and Wada's method, we then conclude that $q(K)$ is either $2$ or $1$, the distinction resting on the fulfilment or otherwise of one of the conditions set forth below:
 	\begin{enumerate}[C1)]
		\item $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)=-1$,
		\item $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)$.
	\end{enumerate}
	An entirely analogous procedure to that of the previous paragraph furnishes the conditions that establish cases $2)$--$i)$ and $2)$--$ii)$.
	\item[6)]  Let $d_1=p_1q$ and $d_2=p_2q$ where [$\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_1\equiv 5\pmod 8$], [$\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_2\equiv 5\pmod 8$],  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. According to  \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity}, we have $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=1$, then $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}=y_1\sqrt{p_1}+y_2\sqrt{p_2},$ for some rational numbers $y_1$ and $y_2$. Combining this with  Table \ref{tab7} in this case, we check that $q(K)\geq2$, in fact at least one of the following square roots $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1q}}$, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_2q}}$, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q}\varepsilon_{p_2q}}$ or $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q}\varepsilon_{p_2q}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}$ is in $E_K$. This such case must be rejected.
	\item[7)] Let  $d_1=2p_1q$ and $d_2=2p_2q$ where   [$\left(\frac{p_1}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_1\equiv 5\pmod 8$], [$\left(\frac{p_2}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p_2\equiv 5\pmod 8$],  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. Using the same argument as in the previous case one can conclude that $q(K)=2$. In fact $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2p_1q},\varepsilon_{2p_2q},\eta \rangle}$ with $\eta=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1q}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_2q}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_1q}\varepsilon_{2p_2q}} \;\text{or}\; \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_1q}\varepsilon_{2p_2q}}$. Thus such case must be rejected.
	
	\item[8)] Let $d_1=p_1q_1q_2$ and $d_2=p_2q_1q_2$ where $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv -q_1 \equiv -q_2 \equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that   [$\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$], [$\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=-1$] \text{and} $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$. According to  \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity} we have  $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$, it follows that the unit $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{p_2q_1q_2}}$ is the only square candidate belonging to $E_K$, because the other two units, $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_2q_2}}$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2q_2q_2}}$, take possible forms that do not belong to $E_K$ (cf. Table \ref{tab8}). By using Table \ref{tab8} and Wada's method we get $q(K)=2$ exactly in one of the following cases:\begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=-1,$ 
		\item $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-1$ and $\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate} 
	Therefore in this sub-case we get   $q(K)=1$ if and only if 
	
	$$\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)\cdot\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1.$$
	Which justifies the third case.
	
	
	\item[9)] Let $d_1=p_1q_1q_2$ and $d_2=p_2q_1q_2$ where [$\left(\frac{p_1}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p_1}{q_2}\right)=-1$], [$\left(\frac{p_2}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p_2}{q_2}\right)=-1$],  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ \text{and} $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. As $N_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=1$ (cf. \cite[Theorem 1]{kuvcera1995parity}), Then by Table \ref{tab8} we conclude that $q(K)=2$, more precisely we have $E_K=\langle{-1,\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2},\varepsilon_{p_2q_1q_2},\eta \rangle}$ with $\eta=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_2q_1q_2}}, \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{p_2q_1q_2}} \;\text{or}\; \sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{p_2q_1q_2}}$. Thus such case must be rejected.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	\item[10)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv 5 \pmod 8$ with $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$, then \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} gives that all three fundamental units of the quadratic subfields of $K$ have norm $-1$. Wada's method then implies that $q(K)=2$ or $1$ according to whether  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_1}\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}\in K$ or not. 
	
	
	
	
	\item[11)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes  with $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv5\pmod8 $,  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ \text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. By \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=-N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-1$, then $q(K)=1$, in fact the only square root candidate to be in $E_K$ is $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}$, but it takes the form $[\sqrt{p_1}, \sqrt{p_2}]$ which is not in $K.$
	
	
	\item[12)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes  with  $p_1\equiv5\pmod8$, $p_2\equiv1\pmod8 $,   $\left(\frac{2}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{2}\right)_4$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$.  According to o \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=-1$, thus $q(K)=1$ as $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}}\notin K$.
	\item[13)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes  with   $p_1\equiv5\pmod8$, $p_2\equiv1\pmod8 $, $\left(\frac{2}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{2}\right)_4$, $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$  \text{ and }  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. Then According to o \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=-N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=1$, moreover $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}}=[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p_2}]$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_2}]$, then $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}\in K$ and $q(K)=2$.
	\item[14)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes  with $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod8 $, $\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_1}{2}\right)_4$, $\left(\frac{2}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{2}\right)_4$  \text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$.  According to  \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=-N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=1$,  and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_1}}=[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p_1}]$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}}=[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p_2}]$, thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_2}}\in K$ and $q(K)=2$.
	\item[15)] If $d_1=2p_1$ and $d_2=2p_2$ for distinct primes  with $p_1\equiv p_2\equiv1\pmod8 $, $\left(\frac{2}{p_1}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_1}{2}\right)_4$, $\left(\frac{2}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{2}\right)_4$,   $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ \text{ and }    $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$. Then according to \cite[Theorems 1 and 2]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{2p_1})=N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=N(\varepsilon_{2p_2})=1$,  and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_1}}=[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p_1}]$,  $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}}=[\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p_2}]$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_2}]$, thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_2}}$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2p_2}\varepsilon_{2p_2}}\in K$ and $q(K)=4.$
	
	
	\item[16)] If $d_1=p_1p_2$ and $d_2=p_2p_3$ for some distinct prime numbers $p_i\equiv1\pmod4$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=-1$, this case is similar to the previous, hence $q(K)=2$ or $1$ according to whether $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}$ is in $K$ or not.
	
	\item[17)] If $d_1=p_1p_2$ and $d_2=p_2p_3$ for some distinct prime numbers $p_i\equiv1\pmod4$ such that $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=-1$, $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=1$\text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_1}\right)_4$. Then according to  \cite[Theorems 1 ]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=N(\varepsilon_{p_2p_3})=-N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_3})=-1$, then $q(K)=1$ since the only square root candidate to be in $E_K$ is $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_3}]$, which is not.
	
	\item[18)] If $d_1=p_1p_2$ and $d_2=p_2p_3$ for some distinct prime numbers $p_i\equiv1\pmod4$ such that $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$, $\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=1$,  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_1}\right)_4$ \text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_2}\right)_4$. Then  according to  \cite[Theorems 1 ]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{p_2p_3})=N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_3})=-N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=1$, thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}}=[\sqrt{p_2},\sqrt{p_3}]$ and   $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_3}]$. Therefore $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}\in K$ and $q(K)=2$.
	
	\item[19)] If $d_1=p_1p_2$ and $d_2=p_2p_3$ for some distinct prime numbers $p_i\equiv1\pmod4$ such that $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)=1$,  $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_1}\right)_4$, $\left(\frac{p_2}{p_3}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_3}{p_2}\right)_4$  \text{ and } $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\neq \left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4$.  Then  according to  \cite[Theorems 1 ]{kuvcera1995parity} we have $N(\varepsilon_{p_2p_3})=N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_3})=N(\varepsilon_{p_1p_2})=1$, thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}}=[\sqrt{p_2},\sqrt{p_3}]$,   $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_3}]$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}=[\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_2}]$ . Therefore $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}\varepsilon_{p_1p_3}}$ and $\sqrt{\varepsilon_{p_2p_3}\varepsilon_{p_1p_2}}\in K$ and $q(K)=4$.
	
\end{enumerate}
Plugging all the above investigations together, we complete the proof of our   theorem.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $K$ be a real quadratic field. The class number of $K$ is odd   if and only if it takes one of the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[$    1)$]
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p})$ where $p$  is a   prime number congruent to $1\pmod 4$. 
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2})$  where  $q$, $q_1$, $q_2$ are prime  numbers congruent to $3\pmod 4$.
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{realBiquadCorre} Let $K$ be a real biquadratic number field. The class number of $K$ is odd if and only if   it takes one of the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q},\sqrt{p})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q},\sqrt{p})$ with $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p\equiv5 \pmod 8$,
	\item	$K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q_1q_2})$ with   $q_1\equiv3 \pmod 8$ or $q_2\equiv3 \pmod 8$, 
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p},\sqrt{q_1q_2})$  with $\left(\frac{q_1}{p}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{q_2}{p}\right)=-1$,
	\item  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{p})$ with $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4]$,
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1},\sqrt{p_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4]$,
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q})$,   $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{q_2})$, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1},\sqrt{2q_2})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2},\sqrt{q_2q_3}).$
	
\end{enumerate}
Here, $p$, $p_1$, $p_2$  denote  primes numbers congruent to $1\pmod 4$ and $q$, $q_1$, $q_2$, $q_3$ denote  primes numbers congruent to $3\pmod 4$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We have two main cases to investigate.

\noindent\ding{229} Assume that $K$ is unramified over exactly one of its three quadratic subfields denote $k$.
Notice that if  the class number of $K$ is odd, then  $h_2(k)=2$. So  Lemma  \ref{realQuadeven1New}  implies that  $k$
 is in one of the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
		\item $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pq})$ or $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2pq})$  with  $\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)=-1$ or $p\equiv5\pmod8$.
	\item $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1q_2})$ with $q_1\equiv3\pmod8$ or $q_2\equiv3\pmod8.$
	\item $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{pq_1q_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p}{q_1}\right)=-1$ or $\left(\frac{p}{q_2}\right)=-1.$
	
	
	\item $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2p})$ with $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)_4]$.	
	
	
	\item $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p_1p_2})$ with $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)_4]$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence, by  class field theory, the class number of $K$ is odd if and only if $K$ takes one of the forms listed in items enumerated from  $1)$ to $5)$ in the above theorem.

\noindent\ding{229} Now assume that $K$ is ramified over each of its three quadratic subfields. Assume that the class number of $K$ is odd and let $k$ be any of of the quadratic subfields of $K$. Thus we have $h_2(k)=1$ or $2$.
It follows from Lemmas  \ref{realQuadodd} and \ref{realQuadeven1New} that we have 
$$K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q}),\quad    \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{q_2}),\quad \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1},\sqrt{2q_2})\  \text{ or }\ \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2},\sqrt{q_2q_3}).$$
Here $q_1$, $q_2$ and $q_3$ are prime numbers congruent to $3\pmod4$ and  satisfy some extra conditions as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
	\item If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{q})$,
 then $q\equiv3\pmod4$ is a prime number. Notice that in this case, we deduce from  Lemma \ref{unitsrs} that  we have $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q}}\rangle}$. Therefore,    Kuroda's class number formula and Lemma  \ref{realQuadodd} implies that the class number of $K$ is odd.
	\item If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1},\sqrt{q_2})$,  then  $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Notice that in this case, by Lemma \ref{unitsrs} we get $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1}\varepsilon_{q_2}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}}\rangle}$ and so $q(K)=2$.  Thus, by Kuroda's class number formula, the class number of $K$ is odd.
	\item If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2q_1},\sqrt{2q_2})$, then  $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Notice that in this case, Lemma \ref{unitsrs}  implies that $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{2q_1},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q_1}\varepsilon_{2q_2}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{2q_1}\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}}\rangle}$ and so $q(K)=2$. Then 
	Kuroda's class number formula implies that the class number of $K$ is odd.
	\item  If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{q_1q_2},\sqrt{q_2q_3})$,  then   $q_1\equiv q_2\equiv q_3\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers. Notice that in this case,  Lemma \ref{unitsrs} gives $E_K= \langle{-1,\varepsilon_{q_1q_2},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{q_2q_3}},\sqrt{\varepsilon_{q_1q_2}\varepsilon_{q_1q_3}}\rangle}$ and so $q(K)=2$. Then by	Kuroda's class number formula, the class number of $K$ is odd.
\end{enumerate}
Hence, putting all of the above together, we obtain the classification stated in this theorem.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{triquawithodd}
Let $K$ be  real triquadratic number field. Then the class number of $ K $ is odd if and only if $K$ is in one of the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item \( \left( \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} \right) = \left( \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3} \right) = \left( \frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3} \right) = -1 \) and
		$\left( \frac{\ell_1\ell_2}{\ell_3} \right)_4 \left( \frac{\ell_1\ell_3}{\ell_2} \right)_4 \left( \frac{\ell_2\ell_3}{\ell_1} \right)_4 = 1,
		$
		\item \( \left( \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} \right) = 1 \), \( \left( \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3} \right) = \left( \frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3} \right) = -1 \) and $\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)_4.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-1$, $h(2\ell_2 \ell_3)=4$ and \textbf{none} of the two units $\{\varepsilon_{2}\varepsilon_{\ell_2\ell_3}\varepsilon_{2\ell_2\ell_3}, \varepsilon_{2\ell_2\ell_3}\}$ is a square in $K$,
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=1$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)_4\not=\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)_4$,
		$h(2\ell_2\ell_3)=4$ and \textbf{none} of the two units $\{ \varepsilon_{\ell_2\ell_3}\varepsilon_{2\ell_2\ell_3}, \varepsilon_{2\ell_2\ell_3}\}$ is a square in $K$.
	\end{enumerate} 
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that $\ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$. 
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_2\equiv \ell_3\equiv 3\pmod4$ distinct prime numbers such that $\ell_2$ or $\ell_3 \equiv 3\pmod8$.
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_1 \equiv\ell_2 \equiv\ell_3 \equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that  one of the following conditions holds: \begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_3 \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $\ell_2\equiv3\pmod4$ and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		                         
		\item  $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2 \equiv 3\pmod{8}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		
		                                                           
		                                              
		
		\item  $\ell_2\equiv7\pmod8, \ell_3 \equiv 3\pmod{8}$, $\ell_1\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$,
		
		                         
		
		\item $\ell_2\equiv3\pmod8, \ell_3 \equiv 7\pmod{8}$, $\ell_1\equiv3\pmod4$  and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
		
		                         
		
	\end{enumerate} 
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_1\equiv -\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv5\pmod{8}$ and
		\[
		\left(\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right),\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right),
		\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)\right)
		\in\{(i,j,k):i,j,k=\pm1\}
		\setminus\{(1,1,1),(1,-1,1)\},
		\]
		                         
		
		\item    $\ell_1\equiv1\pmod{8}$ and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv5\pmod8, \ell_2\equiv1\pmod8 $ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-1,$
		\item $\ell_1\equiv5\pmod8, \ell_3\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-1,$
		
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-1.$ 
	\end{enumerate}
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=-1,$
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3\ell_4})$, where $ \ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_2\equiv5\pmod8,\ell_3\equiv \ell_4\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1,$ 
		
		\item $\ell_2\equiv5\pmod8,\ell_3\equiv7\pmod8, \ell_4\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{2\ell_3})$, where $ \ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv1\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv5\pmod8, \ell_2\equiv1\pmod{8}$, $\ell_3\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		\item $\ell_1\equiv1\pmod8, \ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{2\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv-\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=-1,$ 
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=1$ and $\ell_4\equiv5\pmod8.$ 
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2\ell_2},\sqrt{2\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})$,  where $\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such that one of the following conditions holds:
	
		\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_4\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=1]$,
		
		\item $\ell_4\equiv1\pmod8$ and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
  
                                                                                 
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{2})$, where $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such  that $\ell_3\equiv3\pmod8$.
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such  that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=1,$
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	
	\item $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{2\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv3\pmod4$ are distinct prime numbers such  that one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_2\equiv \ell_4\equiv7\pmod{8}$, $\ell_1\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=1$,
		
		
		
		\item $\ell_1\equiv\ell_4\equiv3\pmod{8}$, $\ell_2\equiv7\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, where $\ell_1, \ell_2$ and $\ell_3$ be distinct positive square-free integers. Notice that if  $h_2(K)=1$, then by Theorem \ref{FrohlichResults}, we have:
$$M_K:=\mathrm{Card}\{p\in \mathbb{P} : p|\delta_K \}\leq 4.$$
Here $\mathbb{P}$ denotes the set of  prime numbers and $\delta_K$ denotes  the absolute discriminant  of $K$. 
Notice that we have $ M_K=3$ or $4$. Thus, we have two main cases to investigate.


\noindent\ding{229} Let us start by assuming that $M_K=3$. 
This implies that  all the integers $\ell_i$ are prime numbers and so we have the following sub-cases:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item Let  $\ell_1 \equiv\ell_2 \equiv\ell_3 \equiv 1\pmod4$ be prime numbers. Then according to \cite{Bulant}, the class number of $K$ is odd if and only if $K$ takes the form in the first item of our theorem.
	
	
	
	\item Let $\ell_1=2$ and $\ell_2\equiv \ell_3 \equiv1\pmod4$ be distinct  prime numbers.
	Notice that $K/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2})$ is a quadratic unramified extension. Therefore, 
	$h(K)$ is odd if and only if  the $2$-class number of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2})$ equals $2$, which is, by Theorem \ref{class2d} (cf. case $D)$), equivalent to the fact that $K$ takes the forms in the second item of our theorem.
	
	
	
	
	
	\item Let  $\ell_1=2$ and $\ell_2\equiv -\ell_3 \equiv1\pmod4$  be distinct   prime numbers. As $K/k$ is an unramified quadratic extension with $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, we have  $h(K)$ is odd if and only if $h_2(k)=2$. So by Theorem \ref{classqrs} (cf. case $C)$),   we conclude that, $h_2(k)=2$ exactly when $\ell_2\equiv 5 \pmod8.$ 
	
	\item Let $\ell_1=2$ and $\ell_2\equiv \ell_3 \equiv3\pmod4$ be distinct   prime numbers. As $K/k$ is an unramified quadratic extension with $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, then  by Theorem \ref{class2qrs} (cf. case $A)-1)$)  $h(K)$ is odd  if and only if $\ell_2$ or $\ell_3 \equiv 3\pmod8$. 
	
	\item Let $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv3\pmod4$ be distinct   prime numbers. Notice that $K/k$,  with $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$, is an unramified quadratic extension. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. Item $D)$), 
	$h(K)$ is odd if and only if $d$ takes one of the forms in $d$ takes one of the forms listed in Item $5)$ of our theorem.
	
	\item  Let $\ell_1\equiv -\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ be distinct prime numbers. Consider the quadratic unramified extension $K/k$, $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3})$. So by  Theorem \ref{classqrs} (cf. Items $B)-1)$ and $B)-2)$),   $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if  $d$ takes one of the conditions listed in  $6)$ of our theorem.
	
	\item Let $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv 1\pmod4$ be distinct prime numbers. Notice that $K/k$, with $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_2})$, is an unramified quadratic extension.  So by  Theorem \ref{classpd} (cf. Item $E)$),   $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if $d$ takes one of the conditions listed in  $7)$ of our theorem.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent\ding{229}	Now assume that $M_K=4$.
So $K$ is in one of the following forms: 
$$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3\ell_4}),\; \; \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})\;\; or \;\; \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_4}),  $$ where $\ell_i$ are distinct prime numbers.  Thus, we have $3$ main cases to investigate. 
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
	\item Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3\ell_4})$. Notice that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})/K$ is ramified if and only if one of the following three congruence conditions holds: \begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv1\pmod4,$
		\item $\ell_1=2$ and $\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv1\pmod4,$
		\item $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3\equiv1\pmod4$ and $\ell_4=2.$
	\end{enumerate}
	Otherwise we have $h_2(K)\geq 2$, and such fields must be rejected. Now, for each of the cases above, we choose $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3\ell_4})$. It follows that $K/k$ is an unramified quadratic extension. For the case $\mathrm{C}1)$ we have according to Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. $F)-1)$ and $F)-2)$), $h_2(K)=1$ if and only of one of the following conditions holds: 
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=-1,$
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	For the case $\mathrm{C}2)$ we have according to Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. $C)-1)$ and $C)-2)$), $h_2(K)=1$ if and only of one of the following conditions holds: 
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\ell_2\equiv5\pmod8,\ell_3\equiv \ell_4\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1,$ or
		
		\item $\ell_2\equiv5\pmod8,\ell_3\equiv7\pmod8, \ell_4\equiv3\pmod8$ and $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	For the remaining case $\mathrm{C}3)$  in this sub-case we have  according to Theorem \ref{class2qrs} (cf. $B)-3)$ to $B)-5)$), $h_2(K)=1$ if and only of one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\ell_1\equiv5\pmod8, \ell_2\equiv1\pmod{8}$, $\ell_3\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=1$,
		\item $\ell_1\equiv1\pmod8, \ell_2\equiv5\pmod8$  and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_3}{\ell_2}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	
	
	\item Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})$. Notice that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})/K$ ramify if and only if one of the following conditions holds : \begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv-\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$ and $\ell_3=2,$
		\item $\ell_1=2$ and $\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4,$
		\item $\ell_1\equiv\ell_3\equiv-\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$ and $\ell_2=2.$
		\item $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv3\pmod4$ and $\ell_4=2.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	Following the same idea as in the previous case, and using the unramified (under all above conditions $C1)$--$C4)$) quadratic extension $K/k$ where  $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3\ell_4})$, we obtain the following investigation:\\
	In case $C1)$, it follows from Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. $J)-1)$ and $J)-2)$) we have $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=-1,$ 
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=1$ and $\ell_4\equiv5\pmod8.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	For the case $\mathrm{C}2)$,  according to Theorem \ref{class2qrs} (cf. $D)-1)$ and $D)-2)$) we have $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[$a)$]
		\item $\ell_4\equiv5\pmod8$ and $\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-1$ or $[\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=1]$,
		
		\item $\ell_4\equiv1\pmod8$ and  $\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_4}{\ell_2}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
  
                                                                          
	
	
	Now for case $C3)$. By applying  Theorems \ref{class2qrs} and \ref{realBiquad} we conclude that $h_2(K)\geq2.$ Then  such field must be rejected.\\
	Finally if condition $C4)$ holds, then from Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. $H)$) it follows that $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if $\ell_3\equiv 3\pmod8$. 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	\item Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_4})$. Notice that $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1},\sqrt{\ell_2},\sqrt{\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_4})/K$ ramify if and only if one of the following conditions holds : \begin{enumerate}[$\mathrm{C}1)$]
		\item $\ell_1\equiv \ell_2\equiv\ell_3\equiv\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4$,
		\item $\ell_3=2$ and $\ell_1\equiv\ell_2\equiv\ell_4\equiv3\pmod4,$
		                                                                    
		\item $\ell_1=2$ and  $\ell_2\equiv\ell_4\equiv-\ell_3\equiv3\pmod4$.
		                                                                     
	\end{enumerate}
	
	
	By the same investigation as in the two above forms of $K$, by using the suitable unramified (under conditions $C1)$--$C3)$) quadratic extension  $K/k$, where $k=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_2\ell_3},\sqrt{\ell_1\ell_4})$ we caracterise eauch case separably:\\
	If conditions C1) holds, then by Theorem \ref{classq1q2d} (cf. $G)-1)$ and $G)-2)$)  we have $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=1,$ or
		\item $\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_4}{\ell_1}\right)=\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\frac{\ell_3}{\ell_4}\right)=1.$
	\end{enumerate}
	
	If conditions C2) holds, then by Theorem \ref{class2qrs} (cf. $B)-1)$ and $B)-2)$) we have $h_2(K)=1$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:
	
	
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\ell_2\equiv \ell_4\equiv7\pmod{8}$, $\ell_1\equiv3\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=1$,
		
		
		
		\item $\ell_1\equiv\ell_4\equiv3\pmod{8}$, $\ell_2\equiv7\pmod{8}$ and
		$\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{\ell_1}{\ell_4}\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	
	                                                                                                                                                                  
	 
	                  
	                                                                        
	                                                                                                                  
	 
	 
	 
	                                                                        
	                                                                                                                    
	                
	
	Finally if the case $C3)$ holds. We have by Theorems \ref{class2qrs} and \ref{realBiquad} we have $h_2(K)\geq 2$. Hence such field must be rejected.\\
	
	                                                                                                                                                         
	 
	 
	                  
	                                                                       
	                                                                                                                  
	 
	 
	 
	                                                                        
	                                                                                                                    
	                
	
	
	
	Hence, putting all of the above together, we obtain the complete classification stated in the theorem. This completes the proof. 
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{duaqdriwithodd}Let $K$ be a real multiquadratic number fields of degree $16$. Then the class number of $K$ is odd if and only if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1}, \sqrt{\ell_2}, \sqrt{\ell_3}, \sqrt{\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ and $\ell_4$ are  distinct prime numbers satisfying, after a suitable permutation, one of the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[$1)$]
	\item $\ell_1=2$, $\ell_2\equiv \ell_3 \equiv \ell_4 \equiv-1 \pmod4$, $\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_2}\right)=-\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_3}\right)= -\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_4}\right)=1$ and $\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1.$
	\item $\ell_1=2$, $\ell_2\equiv-\ell_3 \equiv -\ell_4 \equiv1 \pmod4$, $\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_2}\right)=-1,$ and 
	\begin{enumerate}[$i)$]
		\item $\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1$ and $\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1;$ or
		\item $\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_3}\right)=\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1$ and $\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1;$ or
		\item $\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_4}\right)=\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_3}\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_4}\right)=-1$ and $\left(\dfrac{\ell_2}{\ell_3}\right)\neq \left(\dfrac{2}{\ell_3}\right).$
	\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

Put  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\ell_1}, \sqrt{\ell_2}, \sqrt{\ell_3}, \sqrt{\ell_4})$, where $\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ and $\ell_4$ are  distinct positive square-free integers. Then, the fact that  all $\ell_i$'s are pairwise distinct, implies that there are at least five finite  primes that ramify in $K/\mathbb{Q}$; this Theorem \ref{FrohlichResults}, implies that   the class number of $K$ is even.

$\ell_1, \ell_2, \ell_3$ and $\ell_4$ are  distinct prime numbers satisfying
  one of the conditions in the above theorem.

body_md:
As $d\equiv1\pmod4$, then $\varepsilon_{d}=x+y\sqrt{d}$, where $x$ and $y$ are integers or semi integers :\\
\noindent\ding{229} If $x$ and $y$ are integers then $x+1$ and $x-1$ are not squares in $\mathbb{N}$ and  $x^2-1=dy^2$ (cf.  \cite[First item in Lemma 2]{AzAekhTouCor}). Assume that there is a divisor $\delta$ of $d$ such that:  \( \delta(x+1) \) or \( \delta(x-1) \) is a square in \( \mathbb{N} \). Then   we have  

$$\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
	x\pm 1=\delta y_1^2\\
	x\mp 1=d' y_2^2,
\end{array}\right.$$
where $y_1, y_2$ and $d'$ are integers such that $y=y_1y_2$ and $d=\delta d'$. Then 

$$\delta d'y_2^2=\delta(x\mp1)=\delta(x\pm1\mp2)=\delta (x\pm1)\mp2\delta=\delta^2y_1^2\mp2\delta,$$ then $$dy_2^2=\delta^2y_1^2\mp2\delta.$$
As $d\equiv 1\pmod4$ and $\delta$ divides $d$,  is follows that  $\delta\equiv \pm1\pmod4$. Reducing modulo 4 we get $$  \mp 2 \equiv y_1^2 - y_2^2 \pmod 4 $$
which is an absurd.\\

\noindent\ding{229} If $x$ and $y$ are semi integers : $x=a/2$ and $y=b/2$,  for some odd integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^2-4=db^2$. First of all if $a-2$ or $a+2$ is a square in $\mathbb{N}$, then we have:

$$\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
	a\pm 2=b_1^2\\
	a\mp 2=d b_2^2,
\end{array}\right.$$
where $b_1$ and $b_2$ are two integers such that $b=b_1b_2$. Then $\varepsilon_d=\frac{1}{4}(b_1^2+b_2^2 d+2b\sqrt{d})$, thus $\sqrt{\varepsilon_d}\in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, which is absurd. Therefore, \(a+2\) and \(a-2\) are not squares in \(\mathbb{N}\); hence, a fortiori, \(x-1\) and \(x+1\) are not squares in \(\mathbb{Q}\).


\medskip

Now  if there is some divisor  $\delta$ of $d$ such that  $\delta(x+1)$ or $\delta(x-1)$ is a square in $\mathbb{Q}$. Then as $a$ is odd we have $\delta(x\pm1)=\frac{\delta(a\pm2)}{2}$ which can not be a square in $\mathbb{Q}$ because $\delta(a\pm2)$ and $2$ are coprime and both square free (A rational number is a square in $\mathbb{Q}$ if and only if both its numerator and its denominator are squares in $\mathbb{N}$.).
